summary:
Lima stands under the national framework of Peru, and the national assessment carried by the parent record applies here. No separate departmental or municipal regime modifying that framework was identified in the sources.

Jorge Chávez international airport in Lima had installed signage reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity". The national norm approved in Congress on 2 April 2025 bars such "ambiguous" signage, and article 5 of the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR prohibits entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated, subject to listed exceptions. The inclusive signs at Lima's international gateway fall inside that prohibition, so a trans visitor should expect facilities across the department to be designated by birth sex rather than by identity.

Enforcement of the restriction, as described by LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho, would reduce to security staff judging for themselves whether a woman entering a facility is trans and demanding her national identity card (DNI). The sources document no guidance, oversight or complaint route governing that judgement.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in Lima, reported on 15 April 2025 in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte that the plenary approved the fused bills on Wednesday 2 April 2025, exempt from a second vote. The authors call article 5 direct legislation conditioning basic rights on a "biological sex", a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle, and note that trans people, though framed as aggressors by the rule, are more often the victims of violence and discrimination.

On 12 February 2023 Rubí Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans woman and sex worker, was kidnapped from jirón Chancay in central Lima by the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang and killed with roughly 30 gunshots. The most recent documented killing of a trans woman in Lima in this record is that case of 12 February 2023; no later instance is documented.

The Agencia Presentes report of 22 July 2024 records state inaction that bears on accountability for that case: no official system records victims' sexual orientation, and hate crimes go unsanctioned. The sources record no outcome in the Rubí Torres Silvano case.
tangentialFactors:
The restroom restriction binding Lima followed a short legislative path. The Congress Women and Family Commission approved the Muñante initiative unanimously on 20 February 2025, at which point, per Infobae, the text still required plenary backing; the plenary approved the fused bills on 2 April 2025, exempt from a second vote.

The restriction is national policy enacted by the legislature that sits and operates in Lima, so the department's own institutions produce the rule that governs its transit spaces, campuses and public facilities.

Lima's largest transit hub had already adopted identity-affirming signage before the ban, which shows the inclusive practice the national norm was written to end rather than a practice Lima never had.

IDEHPUCP's analysis records that the rule presents trans people as a risk in shared facilities while its own evidence points the other way: trans people are more often the victims of the violence and discrimination at issue.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Lima live under the same article 5 restriction as visitors: entry to public sanitary facilities is conditioned on biological sex at birth, with listed exceptions, and enforcement rests on security staff assessing presentation and demanding the DNI. The restriction reaches facilities across the department, including those at Jorge Chávez airport.

The accountability gap documented around the Rubí Torres Silvano case is structural rather than case-specific. No official system records the sexual orientation of victims and hate crimes go unsanctioned, so killings of trans women in Lima enter no official count and generate no sanction through that route.

IDEHPUCP at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru published its analysis of the norm publicly on 15 April 2025, authored by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, setting out the equality and non-discrimination objection to article 5.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Lima-specific count of hate crimes, killings or rights violations is sourced. The only figures in the source set, 54 killings and 170 reports of rights violations for 2020 to 2023, are raw counts covering all of Peru with no population denominator; they are carried by the parent record and do not measure risk in Lima.

Whether Jorge Chávez airport has removed, covered or altered the inclusive signage since the norm was approved on 2 April 2025 is not sourced.

No enforcement data for article 5 in Lima is documented: the sources record no instance of an ID check, a refusal of entry or a penalty imposed under the provision, and no guidance issued by Lima's municipal or departmental authorities.

The outcome of the Rubí Torres Silvano case, including any arrest or conviction, is unresolved in the sources. The most recent documented killing of a trans woman in Lima in this record is dated 12 February 2023, and no later instance is documented.

No current Lima-specific figure on the economic or employment circumstances of trans residents is sourced; the most recent study covering Lima in the source set dates from 2012.
